summary: Describes a new RADIUS attribute, Chargeable-User-Identity. A home network can use it to identify a user for roaming transactions that happen outside the home network. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: When you visit another network, your home network gives you a nickname, so the visited network can tell it is the same visitor without learning more.

questions: how does radius roaming billing work
subtitle: A RADIUS attribute that gives roaming partners a temporary billing handle without revealing who the user is.

tldr.problem: Privacy-preserving EAP methods hide the real user name from networks outside the home network, yet those networks need some stable identity to bind a session, bill and limit fraud.
tldr.mechanism: The home network returns a Chargeable-User-Identity (RADIUS attribute type 89) in the Access-Accept. It is an opaque token that the access network copies into every accounting request.
tldr.outcome: Roaming partners can correlate authentication and accounting for one user without learning the user's identity. The RFC says the mechanism does not solve all related problems.

today: RFC 4372 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Chargeable User Identity
sections.content:
Authentication methods such as EAP-PEAP, EAP-TTLS, EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA can hide the true identity of the user from RADIUS servers outside the home network. The User-Name (1) attribute then holds an anonymous identity such as @example.com, enough to route packets to the home network but not to identify the user.

That causes trouble when local or intermediate networks need a surrogate identity to bind a session. They may want to limit simultaneous sessions per user, or to see a willingness to pay and so limit fraud. The Chargeable-User-Identity (CUI) is an alias or handle for the real identity that serves these needs without undermining anonymity.

The home network asserts that the value represents a user in the home network. The assertion should be temporary: long enough to be useful, but not long enough to identify the user.
sections.eli5: Hiding your name is good, but the hotel still needs some way to know which guest to bill. The nickname solves both.

sections.title: Why Existing Attributes Fall Short
sections.content:
The RFC rejects two alternatives. Class (25) cannot carry the CUI because RFC 2865 says clients MUST NOT interpret it locally. Also, a packet may hold several Class attributes, so outside entities cannot tell which one is the CUI.

User-Name (1) is unreliable because proxies may rewrite it while routing an Access-Request. A server therefore cannot assume it arrived unmodified. Rewriting in an Access-Accept is rarer, since Proxy-State (33) can route the reply. Even so, the request and the accounting packets may take different paths, so another way is needed to convey the CUI to the RADIUS client for use in accounting.
sections.eli5: The two obvious places to put the nickname either must not be read or get scribbled on along the way. So a new, dedicated place is created.

sections.title: How the CUI Is Requested and Returned
sections.content:
A RADIUS client (proxy or NAS) that wants the CUI includes a CUI attribute in the Access-Request. On the initial authentication it contains a single NUL character, called a nul CUI. On re-authentication it contains the previously received CUI. A home server that supports CUI and sees a CUI in the request, nul or not, MUST include one in the Access-Accept. If the request has none, the server SHOULD NOT include one.

For a non-nul CUI, the home server MAY check it against the earlier Access-Accept and SHOULD answer with Access-Reject if the check fails. Support is driven by business agreements, so a server may choose not to send a CUI even when the NAS asked. If a client that requested the CUI gets an Access-Accept without it, it MAY treat the packet as an Access-Reject.

If the Access-Accept included a CUI, clients supporting the attribute MUST put it in the Accounting-Request (Start, Interim and Stop). Clients outside the home network MUST NOT modify the CUI. Clients or servers that do not support the attribute may ignore it, as RFC 2865 allows for unknown types.
sections.eli5: The visited network asks for a nickname with an empty note. Your home network writes one down, and the visited network repeats it on every bill and when you come back.

sections.title: The CUI Attribute Format
sections.content:
The attribute has a Type of 89, a Length of at least 3, and a String. The home RADIUS server decides the format and content of the string. The binding lifetime of the reference to the user follows business agreements, for example one billing period. The string can identify one user but may also stand for another chargeable identity, such as a group of users.

Entities other than the home server MUST treat the content as an opaque token. They SHOULD NOT do anything with it beyond a binary equality comparison between two instances. When the attribute only signals NAS support, the string holds a nul character.

In the attribute table, the CUI may appear 0-1 times in an Access-Request, Access-Accept and Accounting-Request, and not at all in Access-Reject or Access-Challenge.
sections.eli5: The nickname is a sealed label. Everyone except your home network may only check whether two labels match, never open them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The CUI format SHOULD be chosen so the real identity is not revealed. The RFC strongly recommends this, and also recommends keeping the binding lifetime as short as possible when the value references a real identity.

Entities outside the home network MUST NOT modify or insert a CUI in an Access-Accept, but the RFC admits there is no way to detect or prevent this. A man-in-the-middle trying to steal service might change the CUI in Access-Accept or accounting packets, though those already have integrity protection.

A man-in-the-middle could also remove the CUI from an Access-Request. The Access-Accept would then lack a CUI and the NAS might reject the session, a denial of service. To prevent this, the NAS SHOULD include a Message-Authenticator (80) attribute in Access-Requests that carry a CUI.
sections.eli5: Make the nickname hard to trace back, change it often, and seal the envelope so nobody can swap it on the way.

sections.title: Diameter and IANA
sections.content: IANA assigned attribute number 89 in the RADIUS namespace to the CUI. For Diameter, the RFC says an identical attribute with the same Type value needs to be defined, and the CUI should be available as part of the NASREQ application defined in RFC 4005.
sections.eli5: The number 89 was reserved for this nickname field so nothing else uses it. The newer sister protocol is asked to copy it.
